\section{Propositions as Types}
\label{sec:curry-howard}

A theorem prover has to decide whether a proof is correct. A proof written in English cannot be checked by a computer, 
and the Curry--Howard correspondence is exactly the concept that connects logic with programming:
\emph{propositions are types, and proofs are programs}.
A proposition $A$ is true if we can construct a term $t$ of type $A$, written $t : A$.

For example, consider the proposition $A \to B$ (``$A$ implies $B$'').
To prove it, we assume $A$ and construct a proof of $B$.
This is exactly a function that takes a value of type $A$ and returns a value of type $B$.
Thus, logical implication corresponds to a function type. Here are three examples, where $\lambda x.\,e$ denotes a 
function taking $x$ and returning $e$:

\[
\begin{array}{rcll}
P \to P
&:& \lambda p.\,p
& \text{Return the assumption.}\\[4pt]
A \to B \to A
&:& \lambda a.\,\lambda b.\,a
& \text{Ignore the second argument.}\\[4pt]
(A \to B) \to (B \to C) \to A \to C
&:& \lambda f.\,\lambda g.\,\lambda a.\,g(f(a))
& \text{Compose two functions.}
\end{array}
\]

The same idea extends to universal quantification.
To prove ``for every $x : A$, $B(x)$ holds'', we construct a function
that takes any $x : A$ and returns a proof of $B(x)$. Unlike an ordinary function type $A \to B$, the return type $B(x)$
may depend on the input $x$. This is called a \emph{dependent function type},
written
\[
\Pi(x : A).\,B(x).
\]
For example, ``every proposition implies itself'' is expressed as
\[
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P},
\]
where $\Sort{0}$ is the type of propositions. Its proof is simply
\[
\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}.
\]

This gives us the central idea behind a theorem prover:
\emph{proving a theorem means constructing a term of the required type,
and verifying a proof means type-checking that term}.
The kernel implements these typing rules rather than reasoning about
truth directly.

\section{Syntax}
\label{sec:syntax}

We begin with a small dependent type theory consisting of five kinds of terms:
\[
t, A, B ::= \Sort{u} \mid x \mid \tPi{x}{A}{B} \mid \tLam{x}{A}{t} \mid t\;s
\]
Here, $u$ is a natural number and $x$ is a variable name.
Throughout, $s, t, a, b, f, A, B, C, T$ (possibly with subscripts or primes) stand for terms,
$x, y, z$ and the other names bound by $\Pi$ or $\lambda$ stand for variable names, and $u, v$ stand for universe levels.
Accordingly, the set $\FV(t)$ of free variables of a term $t$, defined in \S\ref{sec:subst}, is a set of names.

\begin{itemize}
    \item $\Sort{u}$: A universe containing types.
    \item $x$: A variable.
    \item $\tPi{x}{A}{B}$: A \emph{$\Pi$-type} (dependent function type), whose result type $B$ may depend on $x$.
    \item $\tLam{x}{A}{t}$: A \emph{$\lambda$-abstraction}, i.e.\ a function that takes $x : A$ and returns $t$.
    \item $t\;s$: Function application.
\end{itemize}

\noindent When $B$ does not depend on $x$, we write $A \to B$ instead of
$\tPi{x}{A}{B}$. Thus, ordinary function types are special cases
of dependent function types. For example, the proposition ``every proposition implies itself''
and its proof are represented as
\[
\underbrace{\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}}_{\text{proof}}
\quad : \quad
\underbrace{\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}_{\text{proposition = type of proof}}.
\]
Notice that types and expressions share the same grammar.
There is no separate syntax for types: whether a term is a valid
type is determined by the type checker.

Application associates to the left and arrows associate to the right: $f\;a\;b$ means $(f\;a)\;b$, and
$A \to B \to C$ means $A \to (B \to C)$. A function of two arguments is thus a function that takes the first
argument and returns a function expecting the second; this encoding is called \emph{currying}. For example,
$\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}$ has type $A \to B \to A$, and applied to $x : A$ and $y : B$ it is written
$(\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x\;y$, that is, $((\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x)\;y$.

\section{Free Variables and Substitution}
\label{sec:subst}



$\Pi$ and $\lambda$ \emph{bind} their variable: in $\tLam{x}{A}{t}$, occurrences of $x$ 
inside $t$ refer to the argument. The binder's scope is the body only; $x$ is not bound 
in the annotation $A$.


\begin{definition}[Free variables]
\begin{align*}
\FV(\Sort{u}) &= \emptyset &
\FV(\tPi{x}{A}{B}) &= \FV(A) \cup (\FV(B) \setminus \{x\}) \\
\FV(x) &= \{x\} &
\FV(\tLam{x}{A}{t}) &= \FV(A) \cup (\FV(t) \setminus \{x\}) \\
\FV(t\;s) &= \FV(t) \cup \FV(s)
\end{align*}
\end{definition}

The typing rule for application (\S\ref{sec:typing}) needs to replace a variable with 
a term. We write $\subst{t}{x}{s}$ for the result of replacing the free occurrences 
of $x$ in $t$ with $s$. 

The only subtle case is a binder. Consider $\subst{(\tLam{y}{A}{x})}{x}{y}$. The body 
says ``ignore the argument and return the outer $x$''. Replacing $x$ by $y$ 
naively gives $\tLam{y}{A}{y}$, the identity function, which means something else: 
the free $y$ has been \emph{captured} by the binder. Substitution must avoid this 
by renaming the binder first.


\begin{definition}[Capture-avoiding substitution]

For $\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}$:

\begin{align*}
\subst{x}{x}{s} &= s \\
\subst{y}{x}{s} &= y && (y \neq x) \\
\subst{\Sort{u}}{x}{s} &= \Sort{u} \\
\subst{(t_1\;t_2)}{x}{s} &= \subst{t_1}{x}{s}\;\;\subst{t_2}{x}{s} \\
\subst{(\square(x{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(x{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,B
  && \text{(we say that $x$ is shadowed)} \\
\subst{(\square(y{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(y{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,\subst{B}{x}{s}
  && (y \neq x,\; y \notin \FV(s)) \\
\subst{(\square(y{:}A).\,B)}{x}{s} &= \square(z{:}\subst{A}{x}{s}).\,\subst{(\subst{B}{y}{z})}{x}{s}
  && (y \neq x,\; y \in \FV(s),\; z \text{ fresh})
\end{align*}

\noindent Here ``$z$ fresh'' means $z \notin \FV(s) \cup \FV(B) \cup \{x\}$.

\end{definition}


\section{Alpha-Equivalence}

\label{sec:alpha}



The names of bound variables carry no meaning. For example, $\tLam{x}{A}{x}$ and $\tLam{y}{A}{y}$ are the same function, and 
$\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$ and $\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{Q \to Q}$ are the same proposition. Terms that differ only in the names 
of bound variables are called \emph{$\alpha$-equivalent}.


\begin{definition}[$\alpha$-equivalence]
\label{def:alpha}

$\alphaeq$ is the smallest congruence on terms containing, for $\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}$,

\[
\square(x{:}A).\,B \;\alphaeq\; \square(y{:}A).\,\subst{B}{x}{y}
\qquad \text{whenever } y \notin \FV(B).
\]

\end{definition}

This definition is easy to state but not directly executable, since it does not say which names to choose. An implementation 
instead walks both terms in lockstep and remembers, for each side, the list of binders passed so far. A bound variable is 
then identified by \emph{which} binder it refers to, not by its name.

To describe this walk, we use a judgment of the form $E_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq t$, where $E_1$ and $E_2$ are lists of names.
The list $E_1$ records the binders that enclose $s$, from the outermost to the innermost, and $E_2$ records those that enclose $t$.
The judgment reads: ``$s$, placed inside the binders $E_1$, and $t$, placed inside the binders $E_2$, are the same term up to the names
of bound variables''. Two lists are needed because the two terms may use different names for corresponding binders.
For example, comparing $\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{B}{x}}$ with $\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}$ passes two binders on each side and arrives at
\[
x, y;\; a, b \vdash x \alphaeq a,
\]
which holds because $x$ and $a$ both refer to the outer of the two binders. Comparing two whole terms starts from empty lists,
$\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$. The same symbol $\alphaeq$ appears in Definition~\ref{def:alpha} and in the judgment;
the prefix $E_1; E_2 \vdash$ distinguishes the judgment, and Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha} below shows that the two agree.

To say ``the same binder'' precisely, let $\mathit{idx}(E, x)$ be the position of the last occurrence of $x$ in $E$, counted from
the right starting at $0$, or undefined if $x \notin E$. In the example, $\mathit{idx}(x, y;\, x) = \mathit{idx}(a, b;\, a) = 1$.
Taking the \emph{last} occurrence handles shadowing: in $\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{x}{B}{x}}$ the body refers to the inner $x$.

\begin{figure}[ht]

\footnotesize

\centering

\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\quad}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \Sort{u} \alphaeq \Sort{u}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Sort}
\and
\inferrule{\mathit{idx}(E_1, x) = \mathit{idx}(E_2, y) = i}{E_1; E_2 \vdash x \alphaeq y}\rulename{$\alpha$-Bound}
\and
\inferrule{x \notin E_1 \\ x \notin E_2}{E_1; E_2 \vdash x \alphaeq x}\rulename{$\alpha$-Free}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash A \alphaeq A' \\ E_1, x; E_2, y \vdash B \alphaeq B'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} \alphaeq \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Pi}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash A \alphaeq A' \\ E_1, x; E_2, y \vdash t \alphaeq t'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash \tLam{x}{A}{t} \alphaeq \tLam{y}{A'}{t'}}\rulename{$\alpha$-Lam}
\and
\inferrule{E_1; E_2 \vdash t_1 \alphaeq t_1' \\ E_1; E_2 \vdash t_2 \alphaeq t_2'}{E_1; E_2 \vdash t_1\;t_2 \alphaeq t_1'\;t_2'}\rulename{$\alpha$-App}
\end{mathpar}

\caption{Algorithmic $\alpha$-equivalence. By Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}, two terms $s$ and $t$ are $\alpha$-equivalent iff $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$.}

\label{fig:alpha}

\end{figure}



Free variables are compared by name ($\alpha$-Free), and bound variables by position ($\alpha$-Bound). A variable that is bound on 
one side and free on the other is never equal to anything, which is why there is no rule for that case. Because both sides descend 
through binders together, $E_1$ and $E_2$ always have the same length. So comparing positions counted from the right is the same 
as comparing positions counted from the left, and an implementation may store each list as a map from names to binding depths, 
provided it restores the previous entry when it leaves a binder. Using positions instead of names everywhere gives the 
\emph{de Bruijn representation}~\cite{debruijn1972nameless}, in which $\alpha$-equivalent terms are syntactically identical.

The rules of Figure~\ref{fig:alpha} are a different definition from Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, so we must check that they agree.

\begin{theorem}[Correctness of algorithmic $\alpha$-equivalence]
\label{thm:alpha}
For all terms $s$ and $t$, $s \alphaeq t$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:alpha} if and only if $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$ is derivable by the rules of Figure~\ref{fig:alpha}.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The idea of the proof is that both sides say the same thing: $s$ and $t$ have the same de Bruijn representation.
For the algorithm this is almost immediate, since its rules compare positions exactly as de Bruijn indices do.
For Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, the key fact is that renaming a bound variable does not change the de Bruijn representation.
Appendix~\ref{app:alpha} gives the full proof.


\section{Reduction and Conversion}
\label{sec:conversion}

Applying a $\lambda$-abstraction to an argument is computed by substituting the argument for the bound variable:
\[
(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s \;\betared\; \subst{t}{x}{s}.
\]
This step is called \emph{$\beta$-reduction}.
A subterm of the form $(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s$ is called a \emph{$\beta$-redex}, and we also allow this step anywhere inside a term.
A term with no $\beta$-redex is in \emph{normal form}.

Computation can make two different-looking types equal.
If $\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$, then a proof of $\mathit{Id}\;P$ should also be a proof of $P$, since $\mathit{Id}\;P \betared P$.
\emph{Definitional equality} (or \emph{conversion}) makes such types interchangeable by identifying terms that compute to the same result.

\begin{definition}[Conversion]
$s \conv t$ is the smallest equivalence relation that contains $\alphaeq$ and $\betared$ and is closed under all term constructors.
\end{definition}

To decide $s \conv t$, the kernel normalizes both terms and compares the results with $\alphaeq$.
This procedure relies on two facts.
First, $\beta$-reduction is confluent: different reduction orders cannot lead to different normal forms, so $s \conv t$ holds exactly when the normal forms of $s$ and $t$ are $\alpha$-equivalent.
Second, every well-typed term \emph{has} a normal form, so normalization terminates.
The second fact holds for our system, but it is a deep theorem (strong normalization)~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}.
A practical kernel also caps the number of reduction steps, so that a bug cannot make it loop forever.
Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} in \S\ref{sec:algorithm} includes \textsc{Normalize} as pseudocode.

\section{Typing Rules}
\label{sec:typing}

\paragraph{Contexts and judgments.}
A \emph{context} $\Gamma$ is an ordered list of assumptions $x_1 : A_1, \ldots, x_n : A_n$.
It records the type of each variable in scope, and we write $\dom(\Gamma)$ for the set $\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$.
Since \textsc{C-Ext} below forbids repeated names, $\Gamma$ can be used like a dictionary from names to types,
and \textsc{T-Var} is simply a lookup.
Unlike a plain dictionary, however, the order matters: $A_i$ may mention $x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}$, as in $P : \Sort{0}, h : P$.
We use two judgments:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\ctxok{\Gamma}$: the context $\Gamma$ is well formed.
  \item $\Gamma \vdash t : A$: under the assumptions in $\Gamma$, the term $t$ has type $A$.
\end{itemize}
Read through Curry--Howard, $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ says that $t$ is a proof of $A$ from the hypotheses $\Gamma$.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\quad}{\ctxok{\cdot}}\rulename{C-Empty}
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ \Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ x \notin \dom(\Gamma)}{\ctxok{\Gamma, x : A}}\rulename{C-Ext}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort}
\and
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ (x : A) \in \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash x : A}\rulename{T-Var}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \Sort{\imax(u, v)}}\rulename{T-Pi}
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash t : B}{\Gamma \vdash \tLam{x}{A}{t} : \tPi{x}{A}{B}}\rulename{T-Lam}
\\
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{A}{B} \\ \Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash f\;a : \subst{B}{x}{a}}\rulename{T-App}
\and
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash t : A \\ \Gamma \vdash B : \Sort{u} \\ A \conv B}{\Gamma \vdash t : B}\rulename{T-Conv}
\end{mathpar}
\caption{Well-formed contexts and typing rules.}
\label{fig:typing}
\end{figure}

We read each rule from the bottom up, as a recipe for checking a term.

\begin{description}
  \item[\textsc{C-Empty}, \textsc{C-Ext}.]
    A context is built one assumption at a time, and each new assumption must have a type as its type.
    The side condition $x \notin \dom(\Gamma)$ forbids shadowing inside a context.
    Since we work up to $\alpha$-equivalence, this is no restriction on terms: a binder that would shadow can always be renamed first.
    \S\ref{sec:capture} shows why this condition matters.
  \item[\textsc{T-Sort}.]
    Every universe lives in the next one; see \S\ref{sec:universes} for why.
  \item[\textsc{T-Var}.]
    A variable has the type it was assumed to have. Logically, this is ``use a hypothesis''.
  \item[\textsc{T-Pi}.]
    $\tPi{x}{A}{B}$ is a type if $A$ is a type and $B$ is a type once we assume $x : A$.
    It lives in the larger of the two universes, except that it is a proposition whenever $B$ is one;
    $\imax(u, v)$ is $0$ if $v = 0$ and $\max(u, v)$ otherwise (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).
    Logically, this rule says when $A \to B$ and $\forall x{:}A.\,B$ are well-formed propositions.
  \item[\textsc{T-Lam}.]
    To build a function from $A$ to $B$, assume $x : A$ and build $t : B$.
    Logically, this is the introduction rule for $\to$ and $\forall$: to prove $A \to B$, assume $A$ and prove $B$.
    Note that $B$ may mention $x$, and it is kept as is in the resulting $\Pi$ type.
  \item[\textsc{T-App}.]
    If $f$ maps each $x : A$ to an element of $B$, and $a : A$, then $f\;a$ has type $B$ with $x$ replaced by $a$.
    Logically, this is modus ponens when $B$ does not mention $x$, and instantiation of a universal statement when it does.
    For example, if $f : \tPi{n}{\mathsf{Nat}}{n + 0 = n}$, then $f\;3 : 3 + 0 = 3$ (natural numbers are added in \S\ref{sec:inductive}).
  \item[\textsc{T-Conv}.]
    Types that are equal up to computation are interchangeable.
    This is the only rule that is not determined by the shape of $t$.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Why application matters.}
Without \textsc{T-App}, a hypothesis can be returned but never used.
Roughly, the provable propositions are then those whose conclusion is literally one of the hypotheses, such as $P \to Q \to P$.
Composition, $(P \to Q) \to (Q \to R) \to P \to R$, has the proof
$\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{g}{Q \to R}{\tLam{p}{P}{g\,(f\,p)}}}$, which needs application.

\section{Universes: Why $\mathsf{Sort}\;u$?}
\label{sec:universes}

The typing rules of \S\ref{sec:typing} are meant to be rules of logic.
This section first makes that claim precise (\S\ref{sec:logic}).
It then shows that the simplest choice of universes, a single universe that contains itself, makes the system inconsistent (\S\ref{sec:typetype}),
and that the hierarchy $\Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \cdots$ with an impredicative bottom universe, as in Lean, avoids the problem (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).

\subsection{The Typing Rules as a Logic}
\label{sec:logic}

Consider the logic whose formulas are built from proposition variables $P, Q, \ldots$ by implication and quantification over propositions:
\[
\varphi, \psi ::= P \mid \varphi \to \psi \mid \forall P.\,\varphi
\]
This is second-order propositional logic.
Its proofs are natural-deduction derivations of judgments $\Delta \vdash \varphi$, where $\Delta$ is a list of hypotheses.
Each formula translates to a type, and each list of hypotheses to a context:
\[
P^\ast = P, \qquad
(\varphi \to \psi)^\ast = \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast, \qquad
(\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast},
\]
\[
(\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_n)^\ast = P_1 : \Sort{0}, \ldots, P_k : \Sort{0},\; h_1 : \varphi_1^\ast, \ldots, h_n : \varphi_n^\ast,
\]
where $P_1, \ldots, P_k$ are the proposition variables free in $\Delta$ and $h_1, \ldots, h_n$ are fresh names for the hypotheses.
Figure~\ref{fig:logic} places each logical rule next to the typing rule it corresponds to.
Erasing the terms from the right column gives the left column exactly.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{3.2}
\begin{tabular}{@{}r@{\qquad}c@{\qquad}c@{}}
& \textbf{Logic} & \textbf{Type theory} \\
Hypothesis &
$\inferrule{\varphi_i \in \Delta}{\Delta \vdash \varphi_i}$ &
$\inferrule{(h_i : \varphi_i^\ast) \in \Delta^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash h_i : \varphi_i^\ast}\rulename{T-Var}$ \\
$\to$-intro &
$\inferrule{\Delta, \varphi \vdash \psi}{\Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast, h : \varphi^\ast \vdash t : \psi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash \tLam{h}{\varphi^\ast}{t} : \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast}\rulename{T-Lam}$ \\
$\to$-elim &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi \\ \Delta \vdash \varphi}{\Delta \vdash \psi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast \vdash f : \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast \\ \Delta^\ast \vdash a : \varphi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash f\;a : \psi^\ast}\rulename{T-App}$ \\
$\forall$-intro &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \varphi \\ P \notin \FV(\Delta)}{\Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast, P : \Sort{0} \vdash t : \varphi^\ast}{\Delta^\ast \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{t} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}}\rulename{T-Lam}$ \\
$\forall$-elim &
$\inferrule{\Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}{\Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}}$ &
$\inferrule{\Delta^\ast \vdash f : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast} \\ \Delta^\ast \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}}{\Delta^\ast \vdash f\;\psi^\ast : \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast}}\rulename{T-App}$
\end{tabular}
\caption{Natural deduction (left) and the typing rules that implement it (right). Premises that only check that a type is well formed are omitted.}
\label{fig:logic}
\end{figure}

In the $\forall$-intro row, the side condition $P \notin \FV(\Delta)$ guarantees that no hypothesis mentions $P$,
so the typing rule may add $P : \Sort{0}$ after the hypotheses.
In the $\forall$-elim row, the premise $\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$ holds for every formula $\psi$, even one that contains $\forall$,
because \textsc{T-Pi} places every translated formula in $\Sort{0}$ (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).
Hence $\forall$-elim may instantiate $P$ with any formula, as in the logic.

\begin{theorem}[Proofs are terms]
\label{thm:pat}
If $\Delta \vdash \varphi$ is provable, then $\Delta^\ast \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$ for some term $t$.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The figure turns each step of a proof into a step of a typing derivation, so every proof becomes a term.
Appendix~\ref{app:pat} states the theorem precisely and gives the full proof.

The theorem says that the type checker can check every proof of the logic.
For the type checker to be trustworthy, we also need the opposite guarantee: it must not accept a term for a proposition that the logic refutes.
Define $\bot = \forall P.\,P$ (``everything holds'').
No proof of $\bot$ exists: if each $P$ is read as true or false, every rule preserves truth under every reading, but $\forall P.\,P$ is false.
The type theory should agree, that is, no closed term should have type
\[
\bot^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}.
\]
A closed term $t : \bot^\ast$ would prove every proposition, since $t\;C : C$ for every $C : \Sort{0}$.
A system in which no closed term has type $\bot^\ast$ is called \emph{consistent}, and a design for universes is acceptable only if the system remains consistent.

One might hope for the full converse of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}: every term of type $\varphi^\ast$ comes from a proof of $\varphi$.
That is a stronger property, called conservativity, and it is harder to establish here,
because $\Sort{0}$ also contains types that are not translations of formulas, such as $\tPi{F}{\Sort{0} \to \Sort{0}}{F\;P \to F\;P}$, and a term may pass through them.
We do not need it; consistency is enough.

\subsection{What Is the Type of $\Sort{0}$?}

The $\forall$ rows of Figure~\ref{fig:logic} bind $P$ with the annotation $\Sort{0}$.
\textsc{T-Lam} and \textsc{T-Pi} require every annotation to be a type, so $\Sort{0}$ itself needs a type.
Without one, a proposition variable could only be an assumption placed in the context from outside:
\[
P : \Sort{0} \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : P \to P
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.
\]
The left judgment proves $P \to P$ for one fixed $P$.
The right one is a single closed term that proves it for every $P$, and it can be applied later to any particular proposition.
\S\ref{sec:typetype} shows that the simplest answer, that $\Sort{0}$ is its own type, makes the system inconsistent.
\S\ref{sec:hierarchy} then presents Lean's answer, a hierarchy of universes.

\subsection{Type Is Not a Type}
\label{sec:typetype}

Suppose we replace all universes by a single universe $\mathsf{Type}$ that contains itself:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}}
\qquad
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathsf{Type} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathsf{Type}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \mathsf{Type}}
\]
Translate $\forall P.\,\varphi$ as $\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{\varphi^\ast}$.
Then $P$ ranges over a collection that contains $\mathsf{Type}$ itself and every type built from it.
Such a collection is the type-theoretic analogue of the set of all sets, and naive set theory shows that such collections lead to contradictions.
The best-known example is \emph{Russell's paradox}.
Let $R = \{\, x \mid x \notin x \,\}$ be the set of all sets that are not members of themselves.
If $R \in R$, then $R$ fails the condition, so $R \notin R$; if $R \notin R$, then $R$ satisfies the condition, so $R \in R$.
Either way we reach a contradiction, and the culprit is a collection that may contain itself.
Type theory has no membership test like $x \notin x$, so Russell's argument does not carry over word for word.
Girard instead adapted a related paradox about the collection of all well-orderings, due to Burali-Forti, and showed that the system has a closed term
\[
\vdash t_{\mathrm{G}} : \tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P},
\]
and Hurkens later found a short one~\cite{girard1972interpretation,hurkens1995simplification}.
So the system is inconsistent: $\bot$ has no proof, yet $\bot^\ast$ has a term, and a kernel built on these rules accepts a proof of every statement.

The damage reaches the algorithm as well.
Subject reduction still holds, so if $t_{\mathrm{G}}$ had a normal form, it would be a normal closed term of type $\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P}$.
The argument at the end of \S\ref{sec:properties} shows that no such normal term exists.
Hence $t_{\mathrm{G}}$ has no normal form, strong normalization fails, and \textsc{Normalize} in Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} can run forever.

\subsection{A Hierarchy with an Impredicative Bottom}
\label{sec:hierarchy}

The second answer is that $\Sort{0}$ lives in a larger universe, which lives in a larger one still:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort}
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \Sort{2} : \cdots.
\]
No universe contains itself.
A $\Pi$ type takes an argument from one universe and returns a type in another, so \textsc{T-Pi} must also say which universe the $\Pi$ type itself belongs to.
Lean's answer uses the function $\imax$:
\[
\inferrule{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \\ \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \Sort{\imax(u, v)}}\rulename{T-Pi}
\qquad
\imax(u, v) =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } v = 0, \\
\max(u, v) & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
The case split in $\imax$ makes a $\Pi$ type impredicative when its body is a proposition, and predicative otherwise.

\paragraph{Propositions are impredicative.}
If the body $B$ is a proposition ($v = 0$), the whole $\Pi$ is a proposition, whatever it quantifies over.
In particular $(\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$ is in $\Sort{0}$, although it quantifies over all of $\Sort{0}$.
A universe that contains types quantifying over itself is called \emph{impredicative}.
Because every translated formula lies in $\Sort{0}$, the premise $\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$ of $\forall$-elim always holds,
so a universal statement can be instantiated with any proposition, even with itself.
For example, with $\mathit{id} = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}$,
\[
\mathit{id} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0},
\]
so $\mathit{id}\;(\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})\;\mathit{id}$ is well typed, with type $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
The same case makes $\forall n : \mathsf{Nat},\, n + 0 = n$ a proposition once natural numbers are added in \S\ref{sec:inductive}, even though $\mathsf{Nat}$ lives in $\Sort{1}$.

\paragraph{Types are predicative.}
If the body is not a proposition ($v \ge 1$), the $\Pi$ lives in the larger of the two universes.
A type that quantifies over $\Sort{u}$ then lives in $\Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}$, which is never $\Sort{u}$:
\[
\inferrule*[right=T-Pi]
  {\inferrule*[right=T-Sort]{ }{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}} \\ \Gamma, x : \Sort{u} \vdash B : \Sort{v}}
  {\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{\Sort{u}}{B} : \Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}}
\]
This property is called \emph{predicativity}.
For example, the identity on types $\tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{a}{A}{a}}$ has type $\tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to A}$, which lives in $\Sort{2}$,
so it cannot be applied to its own type; a copy at $\Sort{2}$ can.
Each level holds the level beneath it, and in practice a few levels suffice; higher levels appear when one quantifies over large collections, such as the category of all small categories.

\paragraph{Why this is safe.}
Impredicativity looks like the self-reference that \S\ref{sec:typetype} warned against, but it is confined:
$\Sort{0}$ contains types that quantify over $\Sort{0}$, yet $\Sort{0}$ is not a member of itself.
Coquand showed that one impredicative universe at the bottom is consistent~\cite{coquand1988calculus},
whereas Girard's paradox can already be derived once two levels are impredicative~\cite{hurkens1995simplification}.
With these rules the system is consistent and strongly normalizing (\S\ref{sec:properties}).

\subsection{Comparison with Lean}

In Lean~\cite{moura2021lean4}, $\Sort{0}$ is $\mathsf{Prop}$, $\Sort{(u+1)}$ is $\mathsf{Type}\;u$, and $\Pi$ types are assigned universes with $\imax$ exactly as above.
Two differences remain.
First, $\mathsf{Prop}$ in Lean has \emph{definitional proof irrelevance}: any two proofs of the same proposition are definitionally equal.
Our conversion does not identify proofs; adding this would make conversion depend on types, so the simple ``normalize and compare'' check of \S\ref{sec:conversion} would no longer suffice.
Second, Lean has \emph{universe polymorphism}, so definitions can be stated once for all levels $u$, and $\imax$ then matters for level variables as well.
In our system every level is a concrete number.

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\caption{Design choices for universes.}
\label{tab:universes}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}l l X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Design} & \textbf{Quantifies over} & \textbf{Drawback} \\
\midrule
No universes & values only & cannot say ``for every proposition'' \\
$\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}$ & everything & inconsistent \\
Two sorts $\ast : \square$ & $\ast$ only & $\square$ itself has no type \\
$\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}$ with $\max$ & any level & $\forall$ over propositions is not a proposition \\
$\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}$ with $\imax$ (Lean) & any level & normalization is harder to prove \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\section{A Type Checking Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

The rules in Figure~\ref{fig:typing} define which judgments hold, but they are not yet an algorithm,
because \textsc{T-Conv} can be applied at any point.
The standard solution splits type checking into two mutually recursive functions~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}:
\textsc{Infer} computes the type of a term, and \textsc{Check} verifies a term against an expected type.
Conversion is used only where two types must be compared: in \textsc{Check}, and when a type must have a particular shape (a $\Pi$ or a $\mathsf{Sort}$).

\begin{algorithm}[ht]
\footnotesize
\caption{Type inference, checking, and normalization.}
\label{alg:infer}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Function{Infer}{$\Gamma, t$}
  \If{$t = \Sort{u}$} \Return $\Sort{(u+1)}$
  \ElsIf{$t = x$}
    \If{$(x : A) \in \Gamma$} \Return $A$ \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``unbound variable'' \EndIf
  \ElsIf{$t = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$}
    \State $u \gets \Call{InferSort}{\Gamma, A}$
    \State $(x', B') \gets \Call{Freshen}{\Gamma, x, B}$
    \State $v \gets \Call{InferSort}{(\Gamma, x' : A), B'}$
    \State \Return $\Sort{\imax(u, v)}$
  \ElsIf{$t = \tLam{x}{A}{s}$}
    \State $\Call{InferSort}{\Gamma, A}$
    \State $(x', s') \gets \Call{Freshen}{\Gamma, x, s}$
    \State $B \gets \Call{Infer}{(\Gamma, x' : A), s'}$
    \State \Return $\tPi{x'}{A}{B}$
  \ElsIf{$t = f\;a$}
    \State $T \gets \textsc{Normalize}(\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, f))$
    \If{$T = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$}
      \State $\Call{Check}{\Gamma, a, A}$
      \State \Return $\subst{B}{x}{a}$
    \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``not a function''
    \EndIf
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Check}{$\Gamma, t, T$}
  \State $T' \gets \Call{Infer}{\Gamma, t}$
  \If{$\textsc{Normalize}(T') \alphaeq \textsc{Normalize}(T)$} \Return
  \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``type mismatch''
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{InferSort}{$\Gamma, A$}
  \State $T \gets \textsc{Normalize}(\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma, A))$
  \If{$T = \Sort{u}$} \Return $u$ \Else\ \textbf{fail} ``expected a type'' \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Freshen}{$\Gamma, x, b$}
  \If{$x \in \dom(\Gamma)$}
    \State choose $x' \notin \dom(\Gamma) \cup \FV(b)$
    \State \Return $(x', \subst{b}{x}{x'})$
  \Else\ \Return $(x, b)$
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Whnf}{$t$}
  \Loop
    \State write $t$ as a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$
    \If{$h = \tLam{x}{A}{b}$ and $n \ge 1$} \Comment{$\beta$}
      \State $t \gets (\subst{b}{x}{a_1})\;a_2 \cdots a_n$
    \Else\ \Return $t$
    \EndIf
  \EndLoop
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{Normalize}{$t$}
  \State $t \gets \Call{Whnf}{t}$
  \If{$t = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$} \Return $\tPi{x}{\Call{Normalize}{A}}{\Call{Normalize}{B}}$
  \ElsIf{$t = \tLam{x}{A}{b}$} \Return $\tLam{x}{\Call{Normalize}{A}}{\Call{Normalize}{b}}$
  \Else\ write $t$ as a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$ and \Return $h\;\Call{Normalize}{a_1} \cdots \Call{Normalize}{a_n}$
  \EndIf
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} has the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Each case corresponds to exactly one rule of Figure~\ref{fig:typing}, so the algorithm is \emph{syntax-directed}.
    Finding a proof may be hard, but checking a given proof is mechanical.
  \item \textsc{InferSort} implements the premises of the form $\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}$.
    It is also how the kernel decides whether a term is a type at all: $A$ is a type exactly when its type normalizes to a universe.
    A $\lambda$-abstraction can never be a type, because its inferred type is always a $\Pi$.
  \item \textsc{Freshen} renames a binder whose name is already in the context, implementing the side condition of \textsc{C-Ext}.
  \item Starting from the empty context, every context the algorithm builds is well formed, because each assumption is added only after \textsc{InferSort} succeeds.
    A caller that starts from a non-empty context must check that context separately.
  \item Termination depends on \textsc{Normalize} terminating, which holds for well-typed terms by strong normalization (\S\ref{sec:conversion}).
\end{itemize}

The last two functions of Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} define \textsc{Normalize}.
It is built from \textsc{Whnf}, which reduces only the head of a term until no rule applies there, giving its \emph{weak head normal form}.
A term is viewed as a \emph{spine} $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$: a head $h$ that is not an application, applied to $n \ge 0$ arguments.
Since application associates to the left (\S\ref{sec:syntax}), $f\;a\;b\;c$ is the nested term $((f\;a)\;b)\;c$;
following the function side of each application down to $f$ gives the head, and the arguments met on the way, read from the inside out, are $a, b, c$.
Every term has exactly one such decomposition; a term that is not an application is a spine with $n = 0$.
In the system so far the only reduction is $\beta$, so \textsc{Whnf} has a single case; \S\ref{sec:iota-data} adds two more.

\noindent \textsc{Whnf} alone is enough when a caller only needs the outermost shape of a type, such as a $\Pi$ in the application case of \textsc{Infer}.
Practical kernels use \textsc{Whnf} there and compare types lazily instead of normalizing them fully; Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} normalizes fully for simplicity.
Termination of the loop for well-typed terms is strong normalization.

\section{Worked Examples}
\label{sec:examples}

This section runs Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} on three terms and relates each run to the typing rules of Figure~\ref{fig:typing}.

\paragraph{The identity proof.}
Let $\Gamma_1 = P : \Sort{0}$ and $\Gamma_2 = \Gamma_1, h : P$.
Omitting the well-formedness premises $\ctxok{\Gamma}$, the derivation of the opening example is
\[
\footnotesize
\inferrule*[right=T-Lam]
  {\inferrule*[right=T-Sort]{ }{\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}} \\
   \inferrule*[right=T-Lam]
     {\inferrule*[right=T-Var]{ }{\Gamma_1 \vdash P : \Sort{0}} \\
      \inferrule*[right=T-Var]{ }{\Gamma_2 \vdash h : P}}
     {\Gamma_1 \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : P \to P}}
  {\cdot \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
\]
The algorithm builds the same derivation from the bottom up.
$\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}})$ makes the following calls:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=\arabic*.]
  \item $\textsc{InferSort}(\cdot, \Sort{0})$: \textsc{Infer} returns $\Sort{1}$, so the annotation is a type. \hfill (\textsc{T-Sort})
  \item $\textsc{Freshen}$ leaves $P$ unchanged, since the context is empty.
  \item $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_1, \tLam{h}{P}{h})$, which makes three calls of its own:
  \begin{enumerate}[nosep, label=(\alph*)]
    \item $\textsc{InferSort}(\Gamma_1, P)$: \textsc{Infer} looks up $P$ and returns $\Sort{0}$. \hfill (\textsc{T-Var})
    \item $\textsc{Freshen}$ leaves $h$ unchanged.
    \item $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_2, h)$ looks up $h$ and returns $P$. \hfill (\textsc{T-Var})
  \end{enumerate}
  It returns $\tPi{h}{P}{P}$. \hfill (inner \textsc{T-Lam})
\end{enumerate}
The outer call returns $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}$. \hfill (outer \textsc{T-Lam})

\noindent Each call that returns a type corresponds to one node of the tree, and no call uses conversion.
The result is $\alpha$-equivalent to the stated type, because $P \to P$ abbreviates $\tPi{\_}{P}{P}$ and neither $h$ nor $\_$ occurs in the body.

\paragraph{A wrong proof.}
Suppose a user claims that $t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{P}}$ proves $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
The kernel calls $\textsc{Check}(\cdot, t, \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})$, which first calls \textsc{Infer}.
The calls are the same as above, except that the last one, $\textsc{Infer}(\Gamma_2, P)$, returns $\Sort{0}$.
So \textsc{Infer} succeeds with
\[
\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, t) = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}}.
\]
The term $t$ is well typed; it is just not a proof of the claimed proposition.
\textsc{Check} then compares the two types, which are already normal, using the rules of Figure~\ref{fig:alpha}:
\[
\begin{array}{l@{\qquad}l}
\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}} \alphaeq \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{\_}{P}{P}} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad \cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq \Sort{0} & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Sort} \\
\quad P; P \vdash \tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}} \alphaeq \tPi{\_}{P}{P} & \text{by $\alpha$-Pi, needs} \\
\quad\quad P; P \vdash P \alphaeq P & \text{holds by $\alpha$-Bound (index $0$)} \\
\quad\quad P, h; P, \_ \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq P & \text{no rule applies}
\end{array}
\]
so \textsc{Check} reports a type mismatch.
The error is found only because the user stated the proposition to be proved.
A kernel that only ran \textsc{Infer} would accept $t$ and silently assign it a different type.

\paragraph{Conversion.}
Recall $\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$ from \S\ref{sec:conversion}.
Our system has no definitions, so $\mathit{Id}\;P$ below is shorthand for the term $(\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X})\;P$.
Consider checking
\[
t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{h}}
\quad\text{against}\quad
\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.
\]
\textsc{Infer} first checks that the annotation $\mathit{Id}\;P$ is a type.
$\textsc{InferSort}(\Gamma_1, \mathit{Id}\;P)$ reaches the application case of \textsc{Infer}:
the function $\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}$ has type $\tPi{X}{\Sort{0}}{\Sort{0}}$, the argument $P$ passes $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma_1, P, \Sort{0})$,
and the result is $\subst{\Sort{0}}{X}{P} = \Sort{0}$.
The body $h$ then has type $\mathit{Id}\;P$, so
\[
\textsc{Infer}(\cdot, t) = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{\mathit{Id}\;P}}.
\]
This is not $\alpha$-equivalent to $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$.
But \textsc{Check} normalizes both sides before comparing them, and $\mathit{Id}\;P \betared P$,
so the inferred type becomes $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}$ and the comparison succeeds as in the first example.
In the typing rules, this step is an application of \textsc{T-Conv} at the root of the derivation:
\[
\footnotesize
\inferrule*[right=T-Conv]
  {\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \\
   \cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0} \\
   \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \conv \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
  {\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}
\]
The algorithm never decides where to apply \textsc{T-Conv}.
As described in \S\ref{sec:algorithm}, conversion is hidden in the calls to \textsc{Normalize}, which run only where two types are compared.

\paragraph{An exercise.}
Prove $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{P \to Q \to P}}$.
One answer is
\[
\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{\tLam{q}{Q}{p}}}}.
\]
The proof never uses $q$; this system allows hypotheses to go unused.
Running \textsc{Infer} on it by hand, as in the first example, is a good check of one's understanding of the algorithm.

\section{A Pitfall: Variable Capture in Contexts}
\label{sec:capture}

It is tempting to drop the side condition $x \notin \dom(\Gamma)$ and let a new assumption simply shadow an old one, as most programming languages do.
Doing so makes the kernel unsound.
Consider
\[
t = \tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{y}{x}{\tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{y}}}.
\]
The variable $y$ has the \emph{outer} $x$ as its type, and the innermost $\lambda$ ignores its argument.
So the correct type of $t$ is
\[
\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x'}{\Sort{0}}{x}}}.
\]
A checker without \textsc{Freshen} looks up $y$ in the context $x : \Sort{0}, y : x, x : \Sort{0}$ and returns its type, the bare name $x$.
At that point $x$ refers to the inner binder, and the checker returns
\[
\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{x}}},
\]
which says ``from any element of any type, produce an element of every type''.
Given $A : \Sort{0}$ and $a : A$, the term $t\;A\;a$ then has type $\tPi{B}{\Sort{0}}{B}$, a proof of False.
Such $A$ and $a$ exist even in the empty context: $A = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}$ is itself a proposition (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}), and the identity function $a = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}$ proves it.

The problem is the same as in substitution (\S\ref{sec:subst}): a name is moved into a scope where it means something else.
It affects any representation that identifies variables by name, whether the context is a list or a hash map.
There are three common remedies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Reject shadowing outright. This is the simplest option, but the reserved name $\_$ used by $A \to B$ must be exempt and never added to the context.
  \item Rename on entry, as \textsc{Freshen} does.
  \item Represent bound variables by position (de Bruijn indices~\cite{debruijn1972nameless}) or use the \emph{locally nameless} style, in which bound variables are indices and free variables carry unique identifiers. Lean 4 takes the latter approach.
\end{enumerate}
A test suite should include $t$ above and check that the kernel either rejects it or assigns it the correct type.

\section{Properties}
\label{sec:properties}

We state, without proof, the standard properties of this system.
It is a Pure Type System: the Calculus of Constructions~\cite{coquand1988calculus} with a hierarchy of predicative universes above its impredicative $\Sort{0}$,
close to Luo's Extended Calculus of Constructions~\cite{luo1990extended}.
The first three properties below hold for every functional Pure Type System~\cite{barendregt1992lambda}.
Strong normalization is much harder in the presence of impredicativity and needs Girard's method of reducibility candidates~\cite{girard1972interpretation,coquand1988calculus,luo1990extended}.
\S\ref{sec:inductive} revisits these properties after adding inductive types.

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of types]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ and $\Gamma \vdash t : B$, then $A \conv B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Type correctness]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$, then either $A = \Sort{u}$ for some $u$, or $\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}$ for some $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Subject reduction]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$ and $t \betared t'$, then $\Gamma \vdash t' : A$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Strong normalization]
If $\Gamma \vdash t : A$, then every sequence of $\beta$-reductions starting from $t$ is finite.
\end{theorem}

Together these give the two guarantees we want from a kernel.
\emph{Decidability}: Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} terminates on every input, so whether a proof is correct can always be determined.
\emph{Consistency}: there is no closed term of type $\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}$.
By strong normalization and subject reduction, such a term would have a normal form of the same type.
That normal form must be $\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{s}$ with $P : \Sort{0} \vdash s : P$ and $s$ normal.
A normal term is a universe, a $\Pi$, a $\lambda$, or a variable applied to arguments, and none of these can have type $P$ in that context:
the only variable available is $P$ itself, whose type is $\Sort{0}$, not $P$.

\section{Inductive Types: Natural Numbers and Equality}
\label{sec:inductive}

So far the only types are universes and $\Pi$ types.
This is enough for propositional logic, but not for mathematics: there are no numbers to reason about, and no way to state that two things are equal.
Lean provides both through \emph{inductive types}.
Declarations such as
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Nat where
  | zero : Nat
  | succ (n : Nat) : Nat

inductive Eq {A : Sort u} : A -> A -> Prop where
  | refl (a : A) : Eq a a
\end{lstlisting}
make the kernel add a type, its constructors, and a \emph{recursor} that eliminates it, together with computation rules for the recursor.
A general kernel derives all of these from the declaration.
We first add the two types above by hand, which shows the ingredients, and then explain in \S\ref{sec:iota-data} how they become data that a fixed kernel processes.

\subsection{Constants and Definitions}
\label{sec:constants}

Terms gain \emph{constants} $c$:
\[
t, A, B ::= \cdots \mid c
\]
A \emph{signature} $\Sigma$ lists the constants.
Each entry either declares a constant with its type, written $c : C$, or also gives it a body, written $c : C \mathrel{:=} t$; the latter are \emph{definitions}.
For example, $\Nat : \Sort{1}$ below is a declaration, and $\add$ in \S\ref{sec:nat} is a definition.
Before an entry is added, its type is checked to be a type in the empty context, and its body, if any, is checked against that type, as Lean does for each \texttt{def}.

The signature is used in two ways.
First, a constant has the type the signature gives it:
\[
\inferrule{\ctxok{\Gamma} \\ (c : C) \in \Sigma}{\Gamma \vdash c : C}\rulename{T-Const}
\]
where $(c : C) \in \Sigma$ covers both declarations and definitions.
Second, a definition can be \emph{unfolded}: the constant is replaced by its body.
This computation step is called \emph{$\delta$-reduction}:
\[
c \deltared t \qquad \text{if } (c : C \mathrel{:=} t) \in \Sigma.
\]
For example, $\add\;2\;1 \deltared (\tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\cdots}})\;2\;1$, after which $\beta$-reduction continues.
A declared constant without a body, such as $\Nat$ or $\zero$, never $\delta$-reduces.
Like $\beta$, the step may be applied to any subterm.

Constants are not variables: they are never bound, so $\FV(c) = \emptyset$ and substitution leaves them unchanged.
Reduction now consists of $\beta$, $\delta$, and the $\iota$-rules introduced below, and conversion (\S\ref{sec:conversion}) is taken with respect to all three.

\subsection{Natural Numbers}
\label{sec:nat}

Figure~\ref{fig:nat-eq} lists the constants for $\Nat$ and $\Eq{}$ and their $\iota$-rules.
The recursor $\NatRec{u}$ takes a \emph{motive} $M$, which says what is to be built for each $n$,
a value $z$ for $\zero$, and a step $s$ that turns a value for $n$ into a value for $\tsucc\;n$.
The $\iota$-rules say that recursion unfolds along the constructors.
As in Lean, where the recursor is \texttt{Nat.rec.\{u\}}, there is one recursor for each universe level; since we have no universe polymorphism, the level is a subscript.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\footnotesize
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\;:\;}l@{\qquad}l@{}}
\toprule
\multicolumn{2}{@{}l}{\textbf{Constant and type}} & \textbf{Lean} \\
\midrule
$\Nat$ & $\Sort{1}$ & \texttt{Nat} \\
$\zero$ & $\Nat$ & \texttt{Nat.zero} \\
$\tsucc$ & $\Nat \to \Nat$ & \texttt{Nat.succ} \\
$\NatRec{u}$ & $\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\tPi{M}{\Nat \to \Sort{u}}{M\;\zero \to {}} \\ \quad (\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)}) \to \tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}\end{array}$ & \texttt{Nat.rec} \\
$\Eq{u}$ & $\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{A \to A \to \Sort{0}}$ & \texttt{Eq} \\
$\refl{u}$ & $\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a}}$ & \texttt{Eq.refl} \\
$\EqRec{u,v}$ & $\begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}\tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{A \to \Sort{v}}{{}}}} \\ \quad M\;a \to \tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to M\;b}\end{array}$ & \texttt{Eq.ndrec} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}c@{\;}l}
\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;\zero &\iotared& z \\
\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;(\tsucc\;n) &\iotared& s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n) \\
\EqRec{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A\;c) &\iotared& m
\end{array}
\]
\caption{Constants for natural numbers and equality (top) and their $\iota$-rules (bottom).}
\label{fig:nat-eq}
\end{figure}

The same recursor does two jobs, depending on the level.

\paragraph{Recursion.}
At level $1$ with a constant motive, $\NatRec{1}$ defines functions by primitive recursion.
Addition, defined by recursion on the second argument as in Lean, is the definition
\[
\add : \Nat \to \Nat \to \Nat \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\NatRec{1}\;M\;m\;s\;n}},
\]
with the constant motive $M = \tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat}$ and the step $s = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;r}}$.
We write $m + n$ for $\add\;m\;n$, and $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ for $\zero, \tsucc\;\zero, \ldots$.
The kernel computes $2 + 1$ as
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}l}
2 + 1
&\to_{\delta\beta} \NatRec{1}\;M\;2\;s\;(\tsucc\;0)
\;\iotared\; s\;0\;(\NatRec{1}\;M\;2\;s\;0) \\
&\to_{\beta} \tsucc\;(\NatRec{1}\;M\;2\;s\;0)
\;\iotared\; \tsucc\;2 = 3.
\end{array}
\]

\paragraph{Induction.}
At level $0$, the motive $M : \Nat \to \Sort{0}$ is a predicate on natural numbers, and the type of $\NatRec{0}$ reads as the induction principle:
\[
M\;\zero \to (\forall n.\; M\;n \to M\;(\tsucc\;n)) \to \forall n.\; M\;n.
\]
Recursion and induction are the same constant at different levels.
Here the choice of $\imax$ in \S\ref{sec:hierarchy} is essential.
The conclusion $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}$ has type $\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}$, so ``$M\;n$ for every $n$'' is a proposition although $\Nat$ lives in $\Sort{1}$.
With $\max$, it would live in $\Sort{1}$, and statements about numbers would not be propositions.

\subsection{Equality}
\label{sec:eq}

For $a, b : A$, the type $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ is the proposition that $a$ and $b$ are equal; when $A$ is $\Nat$ we write it $a = b$.
Its only constructor $\refl{u}$ proves $a = a$.
The recursor $\EqRec{u,v}$ is Leibniz's principle: if $a = b$, then whatever holds of $a$ holds of $b$.
It \emph{transports} $m : M\;a$ along a proof of $a = b$ to $M\;b$, and its $\iota$-rule says that transporting along $\refl{}$ does nothing.
In a well-typed redex, $b$ and $c$ are both convertible to $a$, so the rule can ignore them.
Lean's primitive recursor \texttt{Eq.rec} has a motive that may also depend on the proof of equality; Lean derives \texttt{Eq.ndrec} from it, and the non-dependent version is enough here.

In Lean, the type argument of \texttt{Eq} is \emph{implicit}, written \texttt{\{A\}} above, and the elaborator fills it in.
Our kernel sees only fully explicit terms, so we write every argument; filling them in is the job of the layer above the kernel (\S\ref{sec:tactics}).

\paragraph{Definitional versus propositional equality.}
There are now two notions of equality.
Definitional equality $\conv$ is decided by the kernel by computation; propositional equality $\Eq{}$ is a type, whose proofs may require reasoning.
The constructor $\refl{}$ connects them: by \textsc{T-Conv}, $\refl{u}\;A\;a : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ whenever $a \conv b$.
For example,
\[
n + 0 \;\to_{\delta\beta}\; \NatRec{1}\;M\;n\;s\;\zero \;\iotared\; n,
\]
so $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;n : n + 0 = n$, and Lean proves this by \texttt{rfl}.
In contrast, $0 + n \to_{\delta\beta} \NatRec{1}\;M\;0\;s\;n$ is stuck: $n$ is a variable, and the $\iota$-rules fire only on $\zero$ and $\tsucc$.
So $0 + n = n$ is not provable by $\refl{}$ and needs induction.

\subsection{Example: $0 + n = n$}
\label{sec:zero-add}

We prove $\tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}$ by induction, using $\NatRec{0}$ with the motive $M_0 = \tLam{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Base.} We need $M_0\;0$, which is convertible to $0 + 0 = 0$. Since $0 + 0$ computes to $0$, the term $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0$ works.
  \item \emph{Step.} Given $k : \Nat$ and $\mathit{ih} : 0 + k = k$, we need $M_0\;(\tsucc\;k)$, that is, $0 + \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k$.
    By the second $\iota$-rule, $0 + \tsucc\;k$ computes to $\tsucc\;(0 + k)$, so it suffices to prove $\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k$.
    We start from $\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;(0 + k))$ and transport it along $\mathit{ih}$ with the motive $N = \tLam{b}{\Nat}{\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;b}$,
    which replaces the second $0 + k$ by $k$:
    \[
    \mathit{step} = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{0 + k = k}{
      \EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;(0 + k)\;N\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;(0 + k)))\;k\;\mathit{ih}}}.
    \]
\end{itemize}
The proof is
\[
\mathit{zero\_add} = \NatRec{0}\;M_0\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0)\;\mathit{step} \;:\; \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}.
\]
The kernel checks it with Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}.
Each argument is checked against the corresponding part of the type of $\NatRec{0}$, instantiated with $M_0$, and every comparison succeeds after normalization.
Writing such terms by hand is tedious, and finding the right motive is the hard part; tactics (\S\ref{sec:tactics}) automate both.

\subsection{Computation Rules as Data}
\label{sec:iota-data}

Figure~\ref{fig:nat-eq} writes each $\iota$-rule as a separate equation, which suggests that every new inductive type needs new reduction code in the kernel.
It does not.
A kernel stores the $\iota$-rules as data in the signature, next to the recursor, and a single piece of code applies them for every inductive type.

Each recursor entry records the position of its \emph{major premise}, the argument whose constructor decides which rule applies,
and a list of \emph{rules}, one per constructor.
A rule names the constructor, the number of its \emph{fields} (the arguments that the constructor stores, as opposed to the type parameters it merely carries),
and a right-hand side $\mathit{rhs}$, an ordinary term.
Each constructor entry records how many leading arguments are parameters.
For our two recursors, the data is as follows; type annotations on $\lambda$ are omitted.
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llllll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Recursor} & \textbf{Major} & \textbf{Constructor} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{Fields} & $\mathit{rhs}$ \\
\midrule
$\NatRec{u}$ & 4th & $\zero$ & 0 & 0 & $\lambda M\,z\,s.\; z$ \\
& & $\tsucc$ & 0 & 1 & $\lambda M\,z\,s\,n.\; s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n)$ \\
$\EqRec{u,v}$ & 6th & $\refl{u}$ & 2 & 0 & $\lambda A\,a\,M\,m\,b.\; m$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The $\mathit{rhs}$ takes the arguments before the major premise, then the fields of the constructor.
For example, $\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;(\tsucc\;n)$ selects the second rule and becomes
$(\lambda M\,z\,s\,n.\; s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n))\;M\;z\;s\;n$, which $\beta$-reduces to the right-hand side of the second equation in Figure~\ref{fig:nat-eq}.

Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf-iota} extends \textsc{Whnf} of Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} with two cases, one for $\delta$ and one for $\iota$; \textsc{Normalize} is unchanged.

\begin{algorithm}[ht]
\footnotesize
\caption{\textsc{Whnf} with $\delta$ and $\iota$. Lines 6--12 are new; the rest is as in Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}.}
\label{alg:whnf-iota}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Function{Whnf}{$t$}
  \Loop
    \State write $t$ as a spine $h\;a_1 \cdots a_n$
    \If{$h = \tLam{x}{A}{b}$ and $n \ge 1$} \Comment{$\beta$}
      \State $t \gets (\subst{b}{x}{a_1})\;a_2 \cdots a_n$
    \ElsIf{$h = c$ and $(c : C \mathrel{:=} d) \in \Sigma$} \Comment{$\delta$}
      \State $t \gets d\;a_1 \cdots a_n$
    \ElsIf{$h = c$ is a recursor with major position $p \le n$} \Comment{$\iota$}
      \State $k\;b_1 \cdots b_j \gets \Call{Whnf}{a_p}$
      \If{$k$ is a constructor with a rule $r$ of $c$, and $k$ has $q$ parameters}
        \State $t \gets r.\mathit{rhs}\;a_1 \cdots a_{p-1}\;b_{q+1} \cdots b_j\;a_{p+1} \cdots a_n$
      \Else\ \Return $t$ \Comment{stuck, e.g.\ on a variable}
      \EndIf
    \Else\ \Return $t$
    \EndIf
  \EndLoop
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\noindent The new cases have the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
  \item The $\iota$ case contains no reference to $\Nat$ or $\Eq{}$. It reads the major position and the rules from the signature.
    These two cases are added to the kernel once; after that, each new inductive type adds rows of data, not code.
  \item The major premise is put in weak head normal form before the rules are consulted, because it may become a constructor only after computation, as in $2 + 1$ above.
    If it does not, for instance because it is a variable, the term is stuck and stays as it is; this is why $0 + n$ does not reduce.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{General Inductive Types}

In Lean, a user never writes the rows above.
When it accepts an \texttt{inductive} declaration, the kernel generates the type former, the constructors, the recursor with its type, and the rules, all from the shapes of the constructors.
For \texttt{Nat}, it generates exactly the entries of Figure~\ref{fig:nat-eq} and the table above.
For \texttt{Eq}, it generates the dependent recursor \texttt{Eq.rec}, from which \texttt{Eq.ndrec} is then defined.
So the kernel's rules stay fixed while the signature grows: one generic procedure turns each declaration into signature entries, and Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf-iota} runs their rules.

The procedure must also reject some declarations.
The declaration
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
inductive Bad where
  | mk : (Bad -> False) -> Bad
\end{lstlisting}
mentions \texttt{Bad} to the left of an arrow in the type of a constructor argument.
Case analysis on it would let one define $f : \mathtt{Bad} \to \mathtt{False}$ by $f\;(\mathtt{mk}\;g) = g\;(\mathtt{mk}\;g)$.
Then $f\;(\mathtt{mk}\;f)$ is a closed term of type $\mathtt{False}$, and it reduces to itself, so it has no normal form.
The self-application is the same kind of self-reference as in Russell's paradox (\S\ref{sec:typetype}).
Lean therefore requires every constructor argument to mention the type being defined only \emph{strictly positively}, that is, never to the left of an arrow.

\subsection{Changes to the Kernel and Its Properties}

\textsc{Infer} gains a case for constants, which looks up the type in $\Sigma$, and \textsc{Normalize} keeps its definition from Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer}, with \textsc{Whnf} replaced by Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf-iota}.
\textsc{Check} is unchanged: it still normalizes both types and compares them up to $\alpha$-equivalence.

The $\iota$-rules do not overlap with each other or with $\beta$, so reduction remains confluent.
Subject reduction, strong normalization, and consistency are known for the Calculus of Inductive Constructions~\cite{werner1994theorie}, of which our system is a small fragment.
The short consistency argument of \S\ref{sec:properties} no longer suffices by itself, because normal forms now include stuck recursor applications;
consistency follows from strong normalization by a more careful analysis of normal forms.
Lean's full theory, with definitional proof irrelevance and general inductive types, has subtler metatheory~\cite{carneiro2019type}.

\section{Tactics: Building Proof Terms Interactively}
\label{sec:tactics}

Lean users rarely write terms like $\mathit{zero\_add}$ by hand.
They write a tactic script instead:
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
theorem zero_add (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih]
\end{lstlisting}
Each tactic is a small program that builds part of the proof term.
Tactics run outside the kernel.
Their output is an ordinary term, which the kernel checks with Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} like any other term.
This section shows how the common tactics construct terms in our system.

\subsection{Goals and Proof States}

A \emph{goal} $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle$ asks for a term of type $T$ in the context $\Gamma$.
The \emph{hole} $\hole{m}$ stands for the term still to be found; Lean calls it a \emph{metavariable}.
A \emph{proof state} is a list of goals together with a \emph{partial proof term}, a term that may contain holes.

To prove $T$, we start from the partial term $\hole{0}$ and the single goal $\langle \cdot \vdash \hole{0} : T \rangle$.
A tactic works on the first goal $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle$.
It \emph{assigns} to $\hole{m}$ a term that may contain fresh holes, and replaces the goal by one new goal for each fresh hole.
When no goals remain, the partial term contains no holes, and the kernel checks it against $T$.
A hole may sit under binders, as $\hole{1}$ does in $\tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}$, and the term that fills it may use those bound variables.
That is why each goal carries its own context.

Each tactic must make sure that its assignment has type $T$ in $\Gamma$, assuming each fresh hole is later filled with a term of the type its goal states.
We write $\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \leadsto \text{new goals}$, followed by the assignment.

\subsection{Basic Tactics}

\paragraph{\texttt{intro x}.}
If $T$ normalizes to a $\Pi$ type, the tactic moves its argument into the context:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : \tPi{y}{A}{B} \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma, x : A \vdash \hole{1} : \subst{B}{y}{x} \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}.
\]
The assignment has the right type by \textsc{T-Lam}.
The name $x$ must not be in $\dom(\Gamma)$; otherwise the new assumption would shadow an existing one, which makes the kernel unsound (\S\ref{sec:capture}), so the tactic must rename it.

\paragraph{\texttt{exact t}.}
The tactic closes the goal with a given term:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals},
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} t,
\]
after running $\textsc{Check}(\Gamma, t, T)$ itself.
The kernel would reject an ill-typed $t$ at the end anyway; checking early only gives a better error message.

\paragraph{\texttt{apply f}.}
If $f$ has type $A_1 \to \cdots \to A_n \to B$ with $B \conv T$, the tactic leaves the arguments as new goals:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : A_1 \rangle, \ldots, \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{n} : A_n \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} f\;\hole{1} \cdots \hole{n}.
\]
The assignment has type $B$ by $n$ uses of \textsc{T-App}, and type $T$ by \textsc{T-Conv}.
When the type of $f$ is a dependent $\Pi$, later $A_i$ and $B$ mention earlier arguments, and the tactic must find those arguments by matching $B$ against $T$.
Lean does this by \emph{unification}, solving for metavariables.
Our restricted version handles only non-dependent arrows.

\paragraph{\texttt{change T'}.}
The tactic replaces the goal by a definitionally equal one:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : T' \rangle,
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \hole{1},
\]
provided $T'$ is a type and $T' \conv T$.
It adds nothing to the term; it only changes how the goal is displayed, and \textsc{T-Conv} justifies it.
\texttt{change} is needed because \texttt{rw} (below) finds subterms only up to $\alpha$-equivalence:
a subterm that appears only after computation must first be exposed with \texttt{change}, as in the example of \S\ref{sec:zero-add-tactics}.

\paragraph{\texttt{rfl}.}
If $T$ normalizes to $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$ with $a \conv b$, the tactic closes the goal:
\[
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \rangle \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals},
\qquad
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \refl{u}\;A\;a.
\]
The assignment has type $\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a$, which is convertible to the goal.
So \texttt{rfl} proves exactly the equations that hold by definitional equality (\S\ref{sec:eq}).

\subsection{Induction}

Let $n : \Nat$ be a variable in $\Gamma$, and let $\Gamma \vdash T : \Sort{u}$.
The tactic \texttt{induction n} abstracts $n$ in the goal to form the motive, and produces one goal per constructor:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle
\;\leadsto\;
\langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{z} : \subst{T}{n}{\zero} \rangle,\;
\langle \Gamma, k : \Nat, \mathit{ih} : \subst{T}{n}{k} \vdash \hole{s} : \subst{T}{n}{\tsucc\;k} \rangle, \\[4pt]
\hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \NatRec{u}\;(\tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}})\;\hole{z}\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{\subst{T}{n}{k}}{\hole{s}}})\;n.
\end{array}
\]
With the motive $M = \tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}}$, the type of $\NatRec{u}\;M$ asks for $M\;\zero$ and $\tPi{k}{\Nat}{M\;k \to M\;(\tsucc\;k)}$, and the result has type $M\;n$.
These are convertible to the types of the two goals and to $T$, by $\beta$.
The construction is correct only if the names are fresh, the level $u$ is right, and no other hypothesis mentions $n$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item The motive binds a fresh name $z$, not $n$: since $n$ is already in $\Gamma$, writing $\tLam{n}{\Nat}{T}$ would shadow it, which is the pitfall of \S\ref{sec:capture}.
    Likewise $k$ and $\mathit{ih}$ must be fresh.
  \item The level $u$ of the motive comes from the type of the goal, found by \textsc{InferSort}. For a proposition it is $0$, and $\NatRec{0}$ is induction.
  \item If another hypothesis mentions $n$, for example $h : n = 2$, the new goals still contain $h$ about the original $n$, and $\mathit{ih}$ says nothing about it.
    The goals are then correct but may be unprovable.
    Lean's \texttt{induction} first moves such hypotheses into the goal (it \emph{reverts} them), so that they are part of the motive.
    Our version requires that no other hypothesis mentions $n$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Rewriting}

Let $h : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b$, and let the goal $T$ be a proposition.
The tactic \texttt{rw [h]} replaces $a$ by $b$ in the goal in four steps.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Abstract.} Choose a fresh $x$ and let $C$ be $T$ with every occurrence of $a$ replaced by $x$.
    Occurrences are found up to $\alpha$-equivalence, not up to conversion,
    and an occurrence under a binder that binds a free variable of $a$ is skipped, since there it denotes something else.
  \item \emph{Check the motive.} Check that $\Gamma, x : A \vdash C : \Sort{0}$. This can fail, as shown below.
  \item \emph{Build the term.} The new goal is $\subst{C}{x}{b}$, the goal with $a$ replaced by $b$:
    \[
    \begin{array}{l}
    \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{m} : T \rangle \;\leadsto\; \langle \Gamma \vdash \hole{1} : \subst{C}{x}{b} \rangle, \\[4pt]
    \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \EqRec{u,0}\;A\;a\;(\tLam{x}{A}{C \to T})\;(\tLam{p}{T}{p})\;b\;h\;\hole{1}.
    \end{array}
    \]
  \item \emph{Try \texttt{rfl}.} Like Lean, close the new goal by \texttt{rfl} if possible.
\end{enumerate}
To see that the assignment has type $T$, write $N = \tLam{x}{A}{C \to T}$ for the motive.
Since $\subst{C}{x}{a} = T$, the term $N\;a$ is convertible to $T \to T$, which the identity $\tLam{p}{T}{p}$ inhabits.
Transport along $h$ then gives $N\;b$, which is convertible to $\subst{C}{x}{b} \to T$, and applying it to $\hole{1}$ gives $T$.
Lean builds a different term, \texttt{Eq.mpr (congrArg (fun x => C) h)}, from the same idea.

\paragraph{When the motive is ill typed.}
Abstracting $a$ can break the goal.
Let $\Gamma = n : \Nat,\; h : n = 2,\; q : n = 0$, and suppose we run \texttt{rw [h]} on the goal $\Eq{0}\;(n = 0)\;q\;q$, a statement about the proof $q$.
Abstracting $n$ gives $C = \Eq{0}\;(x = 0)\;q\;q$, which is ill typed: $q$ has type $n = 0$, not $x = 0$, and $q$ itself cannot be abstracted.
Step~2 fails, and Lean reports the same situation as ``motive is not type correct''.
Without step~2, the tactic would produce a term that the kernel rejects.

\subsection{Example: $0 + n = n$ with Tactics}
\label{sec:zero-add-tactics}

In our system the proof of \S\ref{sec:zero-add} becomes the script
\begin{lstlisting}[numbers=none, columns=fullflexible, keepspaces=true]
intro n
induction n
rfl
change succ (0 + k) = succ k
rw [ih]
\end{lstlisting}
The proof state evolves as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Initially there is one goal, $\langle \cdot \vdash \hole{0} : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n} \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{intro n} assigns $\hole{0} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{n}{\Nat}{\hole{1}}$ and leaves $\langle n : \Nat \vdash \hole{1} : 0 + n = n \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{induction n} assigns
    \[
    \hole{1} \mathrel{:=} \NatRec{0}\;(\tLam{z}{\Nat}{0 + z = z})\;\hole{2}\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{0 + k = k}{\hole{3}}})\;n
    \]
    and leaves two goals: $\langle n : \Nat \vdash \hole{2} : 0 + 0 = 0 \rangle$ and $\langle n : \Nat, k : \Nat, \mathit{ih} : 0 + k = k \vdash \hole{3} : 0 + \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k \rangle$.
  \item \texttt{rfl} closes the first goal with $\hole{2} \mathrel{:=} \refl{1}\;\Nat\;(0 + 0)$, since $0 + 0 \conv 0$.
  \item In the second goal, $0 + k$ does not occur syntactically, so \texttt{rw [ih]} would find nothing.
    \texttt{change} first exposes it, using $0 + \tsucc\;k \conv \tsucc\;(0 + k)$: it assigns $\hole{3} \mathrel{:=} \hole{4}$ with the goal $\hole{4} : \tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k$.
    In Lean, rewriting with the lemma \texttt{Nat.add\_succ}, which states $n + \tsucc\;m = \tsucc\;(n + m)$, produces the same goal.
  \item \texttt{rw [ih]} abstracts $0 + k$ to get $C = (\tsucc\;x = \tsucc\;k)$.
    With $T = (\tsucc\;(0 + k) = \tsucc\;k)$ for the current goal, it assigns
    \[
    \hole{4} \mathrel{:=} \EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;(0 + k)\;(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{C \to T})\;(\tLam{p}{T}{p})\;k\;\mathit{ih}\;\hole{5}.
    \]
    The new goal $\hole{5} : \tsucc\;k = \tsucc\;k$ is closed at once by \texttt{rfl}, with $\hole{5} \mathrel{:=} \refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\tsucc\;k)$.
\end{enumerate}
No goals remain.
Substituting the assignments into $\hole{0}$ gives a closed term, and the kernel runs $\textsc{Check}(\cdot, t, \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n})$ on it.
The term differs from the hand-written one of \S\ref{sec:zero-add} in two places:
it starts with $\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\ldots\;n}$ because of \texttt{intro}, and its step uses the motive built by \texttt{rw}.
Both are proofs of the same proposition, and the kernel does not care which one it receives.

\subsection{Why Tactics Need Not Be Trusted}

The kernel checks the final term, so tactics do not have to be correct for the system to be sound.
A buggy tactic can fail, or it can produce an ill-typed term, which the kernel rejects; it cannot make the kernel accept a false theorem.
The checks that tactics perform themselves, such as \textsc{Check} in \texttt{exact} or the motive check in \texttt{rw}, exist only to report errors early and clearly.
The trusted part of the system is therefore small: Algorithm~\ref{alg:infer} with the extended \textsc{Whnf} of Algorithm~\ref{alg:whnf-iota}, and the signature of \S\ref{sec:inductive}.

Lean's tactic framework is far richer than the one sketched here.
It has metavariables solved by unification, an elaborator that fills in implicit arguments and expands notation such as \texttt{0 + n},
an \texttt{induction} that reverts dependent hypotheses, and automation such as \texttt{simp}.
All of this lives on the untrusted side: Lean's kernel, like ours, only ever sees complete terms~\cite{moura2021lean4}.
