\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}}
\label{app:alpha}

Both sides of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha} turn out to say the same thing: $s$ and $t$ have the same de Bruijn representation.
We first define that representation, and then relate it to the algorithm (Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}) and to the definition (Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}).

\paragraph{Nameless terms.}
A \emph{nameless term} is built like a term, except that binders carry no names and a bound variable is written as a number $\#i$:
\[
d ::= \Sort{u} \mid \#i \mid x \mid \Pi\,d.\,d \mid \lambda\,d.\,d \mid d\;d
\]
Free variables keep their names.
For a list of names $E$, the nameless form $\db{t}{E}$ of a term $t$ that occurs under the binders $E$ is
\[
\begin{array}{r@{\;}l@{\qquad}r@{\;}l}
\db{\Sort{u}}{E} &= \Sort{u} &
\db{x}{E} &= \begin{cases} \#\mathit{idx}(E, x) & \text{if } x \in E, \\ x & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \\[10pt]
\db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} &= \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x} &
\db{\tLam{x}{A}{t}}{E} &= \lambda\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{t}{E, x} \\[4pt]
\db{t_1\;t_2}{E} &= \db{t_1}{E}\;\db{t_2}{E}.
\end{array}
\]
Equality of nameless terms is plain syntactic equality.
Note that $\db{t}{E}$ has the same outermost shape as $t$, except that a variable may become either a number or a name.
Constants (\S\ref{sec:constants}) are left unchanged, like universes, and are compared by name; they add only trivial cases below.

\begin{lemma}[The algorithm compares nameless forms]
\label{lem:alpha-alg}
For all $E_1$, $E_2$, $s$, and $t$: $E_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq t$ is derivable if and only if $\db{s}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $s$, for all $t$, $E_1$, and $E_2$.
For each shape of $s$, exactly one rule of Figure~\ref{fig:alpha} can conclude the judgment, and its premises match the equations for $\db{\cdot}{}$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $s = \Sort{u}$, both sides hold exactly when $t = \Sort{u}$, by $\alpha$-Sort.
  \item If $s = x$, the nameless forms can be equal only if $t$ is a variable $y$.
    If $x \in E_1$, then $\db{x}{E_1} = \#\mathit{idx}(E_1, x)$, and equality holds exactly when $y \in E_2$ and $\mathit{idx}(E_2, y) = \mathit{idx}(E_1, x)$, which is the premise of $\alpha$-Bound.
    If $x \notin E_1$, then $\db{x}{E_1} = x$, and equality holds exactly when $y \notin E_2$ and $y = x$, which is the premise of $\alpha$-Free.
    A number never equals a name, matching the absence of a rule for a variable that is bound on one side only.
  \item If $s = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$, equality holds exactly when $t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}$ with $\db{A}{E_1} = \db{A'}{E_2}$ and $\db{B}{E_1, x} = \db{B'}{E_2, y}$.
    By the induction hypothesis, these are the premises of $\alpha$-Pi.
    The cases $\lambda$ and application are the same. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

The definition of $\alphaeq$ involves substitution, so we need two facts about how nameless forms behave under renaming.
The first says that $\db{t}{E}$ depends on $E$ only through the free variables of $t$.

\begin{lemma}[Agreement]
\label{lem:alpha-agree}
If $\mathit{idx}(E_1, v) = \mathit{idx}(E_2, v)$ for every $v \in \FV(t)$, with both sides possibly undefined, then $\db{t}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $t$, for all $E_1$ and $E_2$.
The variable case is the assumption.
Under a binder $x$, the lists $E_1, x$ and $E_2, x$ again agree on the free variables of the body:
$x$ has position $0$ in both, and any other free variable has its position increased by one in both, or stays undefined in both.
\end{proof}

The second says that renaming a binder does not change the nameless form.
We use that substituting a variable for a variable preserves the size of a term, even when binders are renamed; this is a routine induction.

\begin{lemma}[Renaming]
\label{lem:alpha-rename}
Let $y \neq x$, $y \notin \FV(B)$, and $x, y \notin E'$.
Then $\db{B}{E, x, E'} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y, E'}$ for every list $E$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on the size of $B$, for all $E$ and $E'$.
Write $L_x = E, x, E'$ and $L_y = E, y, E'$; they differ only in one entry, at the same position.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $B = x$, then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = y$. Since $x, y \notin E'$, both $\mathit{idx}(L_x, x)$ and $\mathit{idx}(L_y, y)$ equal the length of $E'$.
  \item If $B = v \neq x$, then $v \neq y$ because $y \notin \FV(B)$, and $\subst{B}{x}{y} = v$.
    The position of $v$ is the same in $L_x$ and $L_y$, or undefined in both.
  \item Universes and applications are immediate from the definitions and the induction hypothesis.
  \item Let $B = \tPi{w}{C}{D}$; the case of $\lambda$ is the same.
    The annotation $C$ is handled by the induction hypothesis in each case below, so we consider only the body.
    There are three cases, following the definition of substitution.
    \begin{itemize}
      \item \emph{$w = x$.} Then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{x}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{D}$, and we need $\db{D}{L_x, x} = \db{D}{L_y, x}$.
        We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-agree}.
        The variable $x$ has position $0$ in both lists.
        Any other $v \in \FV(D)$ differs from $y$, since $y \notin \FV(B)$, so its position is the same in both lists, or undefined in both.
      \item \emph{$w \notin \{x, y\}$.} Then $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{w}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{\subst{D}{x}{y}}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $D$, with $E'$ extended by $w$, gives $\db{D}{L_x, w} = \db{\subst{D}{x}{y}}{L_y, w}$.
      \item \emph{$w = y$.} The binder would capture $y$, so substitution renames it to a fresh $z \notin \FV(D) \cup \{x, y\}$:
        $\subst{B}{x}{y} = \tPi{z}{\subst{C}{x}{y}}{\subst{(\subst{D}{y}{z})}{x}{y}}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $D$, renaming its last binder $y$ to $z$, gives $\db{D}{L_x, y} = \db{\subst{D}{y}{z}}{L_x, z}$.
        The induction hypothesis for $\subst{D}{y}{z}$, which has the size of $D$ and no free $y$, with $E'$ extended by $z$,
        gives $\db{\subst{D}{y}{z}}{L_x, z} = \db{\subst{(\subst{D}{y}{z})}{x}{y}}{L_y, z}$. \qedhere
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The definition compares nameless forms]
\label{lem:alpha-def}
If $s \alphaeq t$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:alpha}, then $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for every $E$.
Conversely, if $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for some $E$, then $s \alphaeq t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the first part, let $s \sim t$ mean that $\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}$ for every $E$.
This relation is an equivalence, and it is a congruence, because $\db{\cdot}{}$ is defined constructor by constructor.
It contains the defining equation of Definition~\ref{def:alpha}:
if $y \notin \FV(B)$, then $\db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x}$ and $\db{\tPi{y}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{y}}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y}$,
and the bodies are equal by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-rename} with $E'$ empty (the case $y = x$ is trivial).
Since $\alphaeq$ is the smallest congruence containing that equation, $s \alphaeq t$ implies $s \sim t$.

For the converse, we use induction on the size of $s$, for all $t$ and $E$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $s$ is a variable, so is $t$.
    If both nameless forms are $\#i$, both variables are the entry at position $i$ of $E$, so $s = t$.
    If both are names, then $s = t$ directly.
  \item Universes and applications follow from the induction hypothesis and the congruence of $\alphaeq$.
  \item Let $s = \tPi{x}{A}{B}$, so that $t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}$ with $\db{A}{E} = \db{A'}{E}$ and $\db{B}{E, x} = \db{B'}{E, y}$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $A \alphaeq A'$.
    For the bodies, choose $z \notin \FV(B) \cup \FV(B') \cup \{x, y\}$.
    Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-rename} with $E'$ empty gives $\db{B}{E, x} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z}$ and $\db{B'}{E, y} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}$,
    so $\db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}$.
    Since $\subst{B}{x}{z}$ has the size of $B$, the induction hypothesis gives $\subst{B}{x}{z} \alphaeq \subst{B'}{y}{z}$.
    Then
    \[
    \tPi{x}{A}{B} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A'}{\subst{B'}{y}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{y}{A'}{B'},
    \]
    by the defining equation, by congruence, and by the defining equation read backwards.
    The case of $\lambda$ is the same. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:alpha}]
If $s \alphaeq t$, then $\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}, and $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}.
Conversely, if $\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t$, then $\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-alg}, and $s \alphaeq t$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:alpha-def}.
\end{proof}

\section{Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}}
\label{app:pat}

\paragraph{The precise statement.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:pat} leaves implicit which proposition variables are in scope.
For the proof we make them explicit and write $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$, where $\Theta$ is a list of distinct proposition variables
and every proposition variable free in $\Delta$ or $\varphi$ belongs to $\Theta$.
The rules of Figure~\ref{fig:logic} then read
\begin{mathpar}
\inferrule{\varphi \in \Delta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta, \varphi \vdash \psi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi \\ \Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \psi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta, P; \Delta \vdash \varphi \\ P \notin \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}
\and
\inferrule{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi \\ \FV(\psi) \subseteq \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}}
\end{mathpar}
The side condition $P \notin \FV(\Delta)$ of Figure~\ref{fig:logic} is now implied by $P \notin \Theta$.
Formulas are taken up to $\alpha$-equivalence, and $\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast$ stands for $\tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$ with $x$ fresh.

The context $\Delta^\ast$ of \S\ref{sec:logic} lists the proposition variables first and the hypotheses after them.
The proof has to extend contexts on the right, so it is convenient to allow any order.

\begin{definition}[Representation]
A context $\Gamma$ \emph{represents} $(\Theta; \Delta)$ if $\ctxok{\Gamma}$ and $\Gamma$ consists of
one assumption $P : \Sort{0}$ for each $P \in \Theta$ and one assumption $h : \chi^\ast$ for each $\chi \in \Delta$, in some order.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thm:pat}, precise form]
\label{thm:pat-precise}
If $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$ and $\Gamma$ represents $(\Theta; \Delta)$, then $\Gamma \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$ for some term $t$.
\end{theorem}

\noindent The context $\Delta^\ast$ represents $(\Theta; \Delta)$ when $\Theta$ lists the free proposition variables;
it is well formed by Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type} below and \textsc{C-Ext}.
So Theorem~\ref{thm:pat} is the special case $\Gamma = \Delta^\ast$.

\paragraph{Facts about the translation.}
Translation commutes with substitution: $(\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast = \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast}$.
This is a routine induction on $\varphi$.

\begin{lemma}[Formulas are propositions]
\label{lem:formula-type}
If $\ctxok{\Gamma}$ and $(P : \Sort{0}) \in \Gamma$ for every $P \in \FV(\varphi)$, then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $\varphi$.
For $P$, use \textsc{T-Var}.
For $\varphi \to \psi$, the induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$,
so $\Gamma, x : \varphi^\ast$ is well formed by \textsc{C-Ext} for a fresh $x$.
The induction hypothesis for $\psi$ in that context gives $\Sort{0}$, and \textsc{T-Pi} gives $\Sort{\imax(0, 0)} = \Sort{0}$.
For $\forall Q.\,\chi$, rename $Q$ so that $Q \notin \dom(\Gamma)$.
\textsc{T-Sort} gives $\Gamma \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}$, so $\Gamma, Q : \Sort{0}$ is well formed,
and \textsc{T-Pi} with the induction hypothesis for $\chi$ gives $\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}$.
\end{proof}

\noindent The last case is where impredicativity is used. With $\max$ in place of $\imax$, $(\forall Q.\,\chi)^\ast$ would live in $\Sort{1}$,
and the $\forall$-elim case below would hold only for formulas $\psi$ without $\forall$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pat-precise}]
By induction on the derivation of $\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi$, for all $\Gamma$ at once.
Each case builds the typing derivation shown in the right column of Figure~\ref{fig:logic}.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Hypothesis.} $\Gamma$ contains $h : \varphi^\ast$, so $\Gamma \vdash h : \varphi^\ast$ by \textsc{T-Var}.
  \item \emph{$\to$-intro.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type}, $\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
    For a fresh $h$, the context $\Gamma, h : \varphi^\ast$ is well formed and represents $(\Theta; \Delta, \varphi)$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma, h : \varphi^\ast \vdash t : \psi^\ast$,
    and \textsc{T-Lam} gives $\Gamma \vdash \tLam{h}{\varphi^\ast}{t} : \tPi{h}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$.
    This type is $\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast$, since the free variables of $\psi^\ast$ are proposition variables and $h$ is not one of them.
  \item \emph{$\to$-elim.} The induction hypotheses give $\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}$ with $x \notin \FV(\psi^\ast)$ and $\Gamma \vdash a : \varphi^\ast$.
    \textsc{T-App} gives $\Gamma \vdash f\;a : \subst{\psi^\ast}{x}{a} = \psi^\ast$.
  \item \emph{$\forall$-intro.} Renaming $P$ if necessary, assume $P \notin \dom(\Gamma)$;
    a routine induction shows that renaming a variable of $\Theta$ to a fresh one preserves derivations.
    By \textsc{T-Sort} and \textsc{C-Ext}, $\Gamma, P : \Sort{0}$ is well formed, and it represents $(\Theta, P; \Delta)$.
    The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma, P : \Sort{0} \vdash t : \varphi^\ast$,
    and \textsc{T-Lam} gives $\Gamma \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{t} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$.
  \item \emph{$\forall$-elim.} The induction hypothesis gives $\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}$,
    and Lemma~\ref{lem:formula-type} gives $\Gamma \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}$.
    \textsc{T-App} gives $\Gamma \vdash f\;\psi^\ast : \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast} = (\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast$. \qedhere
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}
